prime.problem: A training run ends with a log full of numbers. Without a fair baseline and a sense of how noisy each score is, you can't tell a real win from a home-field advantage, a leaked test or plain luck.
prime.fits: This is the payoff of the whole lecture. The data card built the scorecards (val loss on a held-out shard, HellaSwag); this card reads them after the 10B-token run and asks how far to trust them.
expect: validation loss vs the GPT-2 checkpoint's 3.2924
caveats: distribution shift, leakage, no shuffling
the cost of 10B tokens: 8×A100 vs your M3
prime.goal: Read a run's train, val and HellaSwag streams against the baselines, say which comparisons are fair and how big the noise is, and explain why the full run needs a rented GPU.

attend: Why can a model trained on 10× fewer tokens than GPT-2 still beat it on HellaSwag, and which part of that win might be unfair?
Why does beating GPT-2's 3.2924 val loss on FineWeb-Edu say less than beating it on HellaSwag?
How many HellaSwag examples do you need before a 0.5-point gap means anything?
What in the loss curve hints that the data wasn't shuffled, and what fix does Karpathy suggest?
Where does the 1.9 h vs 89 days gap come from, and which number in it is measured on your machine?

must: GPT-2 trained on WebText, ours on FineWeb-Edu → the val shard is our distribution → lower val loss is partly home advantage → a task neither model trained on (HellaSwag) is the fairer head-to-head
Accuracy on n examples has noise SE = √(p(1−p)/n) → n = 10,042 gives ±0.47 points, n = 20 gives ±9.7 → 33.24 vs 33.7 is about one SE ("almost GPT-3"), while 29.4 → 33.24 is about 8 SE (a real win)

Better-curated data (educational text) → more signal per token → 10B tokens beat GPT-2's ~100B on HellaSwag → but a test that leaked into the web crawl would inflate the same score, so the win carries a caveat

10B tokens ÷ tokens per second = wall time → ~1.5M tok/s on 8×A100 gives ~1.9 h, ~1,300 tok/s on the M3 gives ~89 days (≈1,150× slower) → you do the full run on a rented GPU and use the laptop to check the plumbing
elevated: The loop only appends step stream value lines to log.txt and a separate notebook plots them → the run needs no supervision, and you can judge an overnight run (or re-plot one) from the text file alone

The data is read in a fixed shard order with no shuffling → the same documents come round at the same point every epoch → a periodic wobble in the loss that looks like a training problem but is really a data-order artefact
reference: eval cadence: every 250 steps, 20 val batches; checkpoint every 5000 steps
llm.c ~223k vs PyTorch ~185k tok/s on one GPU

compress.prompt: From memory, write 4–5 sentences on what the 10B-token run achieved and how much of it you'd believe. Or sketch the scoreboard (random, GPT-2, ours, GPT-3) and annotate each gap with its size in standard errors.
checklist: val loss drops below the GPT-2 checkpoint's 3.2924 on the FineWeb-Edu val shard, but that's partly a home game
HellaSwag passes GPT-2's 29.4% at 10B tokens and reaches 33.24% at 40B, vs GPT-3 124M's 33.7%
with 10,042 examples SE ≈ 0.47 points: the GPT-3 gap is noise-sized and the GPT-2 gap isn't
caveats: different data distribution, possible HellaSwag leak, unshuffled data (periodic loss)
10× fewer tokens than GPT-2, thanks to better data
cost: ~2 h on 8×A100, ~89 days on the M3

retrieve.q: Explain why Karpathy puts two different scorecards (val loss and HellaSwag) on the results plot instead of trusting one.
answer: val loss is on our own training distribution, so it favours our model over GPT-2
HellaSwag is an outside task neither model trained on, so it's a fairer head-to-head
val loss is smooth and cheap every 250 steps; HellaSwag moves slowly and is noisy per point
agreement between the two is what makes the claim believable

retrieve.q: Walk through how one line of the HellaSwag plot is produced, from the training loop to the dashed baseline.
answer: every 250 steps the loop scores all 10,042 examples: the lowest per-token ending loss is the prediction
it writes step hella acc_norm to log.txt
play.ipynb parses the lines into a stream {step: value} and sorts it
plots it against dashed lines at 0.294463 (GPT-2) and 0.337 (GPT-3)

retrieve.q: Your laptop's quick run went from 3/20 to 4/20 on HellaSwag. A teammate says the model is learning common sense. What do you say, and what would it take to check the claim?
answer: SE with n = 20 is about ±9.7 points; a one-example change is 5 points
so the change is noise, and 102,400 tokens is too little training to expect a real gain
you need the full 10,042 examples (±0.47) and a much longer run
the full eval costs ~17 min on the M3, so it's a trade of eval time against certainty

retrieve.q: You have $10 and a laptop. Which parts of this lecture's final step do you run where, and why?
answer: the laptop runs --quick to prove the loop, logging, evals and parser work
the 10B-token run goes to a rented 8×A100 box (~1–2 h, README ~$10)
on the M3, 10B tokens at ~1,300 tok/s takes ~89 days

compare.q: That card builds the scorecards (val shard, HellaSwag completion scoring) and this card reads them. Which design choices made there decide how much you can trust the numbers here?
answer: holding out shard 0 as val → val loss measures generalisation within FineWeb-Edu, not across datasets
completion-style acc_norm → a small model can be scored at all, with length-normalised loss
the size of the val set → the noise level of every comparison
the dataset choice (FineWeb-Edu) → both the 10× token efficiency and the home-field caveat

compare.q: Crushing one batch to loss 0.36 and beating GPT-2's val loss both show a loss going down. What does each prove, and how would each mislead you if you read it as the other?
answer: overfitting one batch proves the plumbing (gradients flow, the optimizer works) and says nothing about generalisation
a held-out val loss below a baseline is evidence of real learning
read an overfit loss as quality and you fool yourself; read a val loss as a plumbing check and you waste a 2-hour run finding bugs

compare.q: The makemore MLP used a train/dev/test split of one dataset. How is comparing against an outside checkpoint (GPT-2) on our val shard different, and what new failure does that bring?
answer: splits of one dataset compare models on the same distribution
GPT-2 trained on different data, so our val shard is off-distribution for it
new failure: a distribution-shift win that looks like a quality win
fix: add an external task (HellaSwag) that neither model trained on

predict.q: Karpathy suggests shuffling documents and shards every epoch for the 40B run. What would you expect to change in the train-loss curve and in the final HellaSwag, and which of the two changes would you be more confident about?
predict.answer: The periodic wobble in the train loss should flatten, because the same documents no longer arrive at the same point in every epoch. That's the confident prediction, since it follows directly from the cause. Any HellaSwag change is less certain: a shuffle mostly affects later epochs, the effect could easily be under one SE (±0.47 points), and you'd need to rerun the whole thing to see it.

apply.task: Run python labs/train_gpt2.py --quick, then python labs/results.py --plot, and open labs/results.png. From the log, compute the standard error of the final HellaSwag score, and the number of 2,048-token quick runs it would take to see 10B tokens.
apply.done: Your plot shows train and val falling from about 10.9 (val 10.9518 → 7.9795) with the dashed 3.2924 far below. SE at p = 0.2, n = 20 is √(0.2 × 0.8 / 20) = 0.089 (±8.9 points), and 19,073 × 2<sup>19</sup> / 102,400 ≈ 97,654 quick runs.
apply.hint: One quick run is 50 steps × 2,048 tokens = 102,400 tokens. The final hella line in the log is 49 hella 0.2000.
